result:
There is an idea I've been turning over in my head for years, and it doesn't have a good name. The best name I have for it is Maintenance.

We love beginnings. We love creation stories, groundbreakings, launches, grand openings. We love the person who invents something, who builds the first version, who plants the flag. We give prizes to the architects and the founders and the discoverers. We have entire sections of bookstores dedicated to origin stories.

What we don't celebrate, almost at all, is the work of keeping things going.

I think about this because almost everything that matters in my life is a maintenance project, not a creation project. My health isn't something I built once and was done with. It's something I maintain with sleep and water and walks I don't always want to take. My friendships aren't mountains I climbed and then got to plant a flag on forever. They are gardens. If I don't weed and water and show up, they go quiet.

For a long time I thought this was a flaw in me. That I wasn't building enough new things. That I was stuck doing dishes and answering emails and having the same difficult conversation with the same person for the third time. I wanted to be an inventor. It took me years to realize I actually wanted to be a caretaker.

Think about the world around you that actually works. The elevator in your building that simply arrives when you call it. The sidewalk that is not covered in snow. The tap water that's clear. The library where the books are back in the right order even though a hundred kids pulled them all out yesterday. None of that is magic. None of it is self-sustaining.

Someone knows that elevator's particular groan. Someone woke up at four in the morning to salt that road. Someone paid the water bill and fixed the pipe and replaced the filter. Someone, probably underpaid and probably tired, put those picture books back.

My grandfather was a man like that. He never built a house, but he kept one house alive for fifty-two years. He could listen to a refrigerator and tell you what was wrong with it. He had a coffee can full of screws that didn't match anything, but he kept them anyway because "you never know." When the screen door ripped, he didn't replace the door. He re-screened it. He stretched the new mesh tight with these little black hands, his knuckles swollen, and rolled the little rubber spline back into the groove with a tiny wheeled tool. It took him all afternoon. I was seven and I thought it was boring. I wanted to go to the hardware store and buy a brand new door. 

He patted the finished screen and said, "Good as new, but better, because it's still ours."

I didn't understand that until much later.

There is a Japanese concept called *wabi-sabi* that gets mistranslated a lot as finding beauty in imperfection. It's more about finding beauty in impermanence and incompleteness and the cycle of wear and repair. A bowl that has been broken and mended with gold - kintsugi - is not beautiful *despite* being broken. It is beautiful because someone paid attention to its history. Someone decided it was worth keeping.

We live in a world that is obsessed with replacement. It's often cheaper and faster to replace than to repair. My phone slows down, I am told to get a new one. My jacket tears, it's easier to order a new one than to darn it. The apps I use are constantly reinventing themselves, adding features, redesigning, never settling. The message underneath is subtle but constant: the new is better than the old. The start is more exciting than the continuation.

But continuation is where all the meaning is.

Consider a city. A city is not built and then finished. A city is a 24-hour maintenance project so enormous it becomes invisible. There's a crew that does nothing but drive around and fill potholes. There's a person whose entire job is to make sure the traffic lights stay synchronized. The sewage system, the power grid, the public park with its grass that grows whether you want it to or not. If maintenance stopped for one week, the city would begin to fold in on itself. In two weeks, it would be unpleasant. In a month, it would be uninhabitable. The city isn't the buildings. The city is the agreement to keep caring for the buildings.

I think about software the same way, because that's part of the world I live in. People imagine that writing a program is like writing a book - you finish it and it's done. It's not. It's like planting a forest. The moment you write it, it starts to rot around the edges. The world changes, the operating system updates, the way people use it shifts. Ninety percent of programming is not writing new code; it's reading old code and trying to understand what the person before you was thinking, and then gently, carefully fixing it without breaking the other things that depend on it. It's custodial work. And the best programmers I've known aren't the flashiest geniuses. They are the most patient caretakers.

Maybe that's why we struggle with relationships and with our planet. We treat them like products we can launch and then move on from, instead of gardens we have to tend every day.

To maintain something is to make a quiet, radical statement: This is worth the trouble. This will not be thrown away. I will be here tomorrow too.

There is humility in it, because maintenance work is rarely seen. No one claps when the floor is swept again. No one throws a parade for the person who remembers to check in on a grieving friend three months after the funeral, when everyone else has moved on. But it is also deeply optimistic. To repair something is to believe that the future will come and that there will be someone there to use it.

Lately I've been trying to practice noticing maintenance in the wild. I notice the crossing guard who knows every kid's name. I notice my neighbor who picks up trash on his walk not because it's his trash, but because it's his block. I notice my friend who always refills the ice tray. I notice the way a dentist's office has plants that someone waters.

I try to do it myself, in small ways. I wipe down the sink even when I'm the only one who will see it. I reread old letters instead of always looking for new information. I mend. I tidy the code. I call my sister back.

It's not glamorous. Some days it feels endless. The dishes will get dirty again in exactly six hours. The inbox will never stay empty. The floor will get dusty. The anxiety will come back next week.

But there is a kind of peace in deciding to be the person who stays. Who doesn't need the novelty to keep caring. Who knows that "good as new, but better, because it's still ours" is the real prize.

If you have something in your life that is still working because you have quietly, without applause, kept it working -- a sobriety, a marriage, a houseplant, a neighborhood, a small business, your own curiosity -- I want you to know that I think you are doing the most important work there is.

You are holding the world together.
